what_this_is: Hindsight's own scenarios are generated by code in this repository, so they cannot show whether it works on data it did not create. This is a committed dataset in a different domain, with different column names and a different leak mechanism, audited by the same deterministic routes.

dataset.decision: Should the retention team intervene before this subscriber churns?
dataset.leak: plan_changes_to_date is a running counter, and the training table joined in every change ever recorded - including the downgrade a customer makes while cancelling. Before the decision it is close to noise; after it, nearly the label.

files.name: retention_decisions.csv
files.what: One row per subscriber: the decision, the outcome, and what was knowable at the time

files.name: plan_change_history.csv
files.what: A running count of plan changes, each row stamped with when it was recorded

files.name: feature_snapshots.csv
files.what: The same facts as a wide feature table, one row per subscriber per as-of date

files.name: scenario.json
files.what: Maps those column names onto the audit contract

files.name: scenario_wide.json
files.what: The wide-table variant, with the sweep candidates

wide_table_agrees.why_it_matters: Most feature stores are wide - one row per entity per as-of date - rather than an event log. Two shapes of the same facts must not produce two answers.

sweep.how_to_read_this: Ranking is triage, not a verdict. A feature high in this list had most of its advantage removed by the cutoff, which is where to look first. Confirming a defect still requires the deterministic routes, one feature at a time. Note that ranking by importance would put the legitimate control near the top instead.
sweep.the_trap: support_tickets_snapshot scores far above the baseline and loses nothing to the cutoff. Ranked by importance it would sit near the top; ranked by advantage lost it is correctly at zero.
